# Hands-on R Lab

**October 22, 2026 | 1:00-1:30 PM Eastern**

What is the effect of district adoption of a gifted education program on district-level achievement?
These are simulated teaching examples, not estimates from the actual gifted education study.

[Download the R script](code/workshop_lab.R) · [Download the R Markdown](workshop.Rmd) · [Data and codebook](data.html)


## 1. Set Up R

For help installing R and RStudio, see [Posit's setup page](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/).
R performs calculations; RStudio provides an interface for code and results.

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| readr | Import CSVs with read_csv(). |
| dplyr | Select observations, create variables, and summarize data. |
| fixest | Estimate regressions and fixed-effects models with feols(). |
| did | Estimate and aggregate cohort-time treatment effects. |

**fixest is the package; feols() is its linear-regression function.**
See the [function documentation](https://lrberge.github.io/fixest/reference/feols.html).

```{r install, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
# Install once.
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "fixest", "did"))
```

```{r packages}
# Load for each session.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(fixest)
library(did)
```

## 2. Load the Data

Our simulation study examines statistical power and estimator performance using **27 state panels
calibrated to Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) district achievement data**. Pure-data and
empirical-data simulations assess how sample size, outcome variability, serial correlation,
and treatment design affect our ability to detect effects.

This lab adapts the pure-data approach using **Texas's parameters: 832 simulated districts
over seven years**, without adjustment covariates. These are generated outcomes, not actual
Texas district records. The simulation manuscript is a working draft; a public link is not yet included.

Place the downloaded CSV files in your R project folder:

```{r import}
simple <- read_csv("simple_did_district.csv")
staggered <- read_csv("staggered_did_district.csv")
```

**read_csv() comes from readr.** Each row is one district in one year.
We use outcome_raw, measured in illustrative score points.
It equals 50 + 10 times outcome_std; a 0.20-SD effect equals 2 score points.
The full untreated Texas panel defines the reference mean and SD before treatment effects are added.

## 3. Check Treatment Timing

Use **dplyr** to count districts by first treatment year:

```{r counts}
simple %>%
  distinct(district_id, treatment_start_year) %>%
  count(treatment_start_year, name = "districts")
staggered %>%
  distinct(district_id, treatment_start_year) %>%
  count(treatment_start_year, name = "districts")
```

**distinct()** keeps one record per district and adoption year; **count()** counts districts in
each group. Read **%>%** as "then." Zero codes never treated; treatment stays on after adoption.

The Texas traditional panel has 416 adopting and 416 never-treated districts.
The staggered panel has 208 Year 5 adopters, 208 Year 6 adopters, and 416 never-treated districts.

## 4. Estimate the Classic Two-by-Two DID

Use Year 4, immediately before adoption, and Year 5, the first treated year.
Following the slides:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}_{2\times2}
=(\overline Y_{G,\mathrm{post}}-\overline Y_{G,\mathrm{pre}})
-(\overline Y_{C,\mathrm{post}}-\overline Y_{C,\mathrm{pre}})
$$

$G$ is the treated group, $C$ the control group, and $\overline Y$ a group mean.
Under parallel trends and no anticipation, the control change supplies the untreated change
for the treated group. Estimate the contrast using the slides' TWFE equation:

$$
Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\beta D_{it}+u_{it}
$$

```{r two-period}
two_period <- simple %>%
  filter(year %in% c(4, 5))
model_2x2 <- feols(
  outcome_raw ~ treated | district_id + year,
  data = two_period,
  vcov = ~ district_id
)
summary(model_2x2)
```

**filter() comes from dplyr; feols() comes from fixest.**

| Equation | R variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_{it}$ | outcome_raw | District achievement outcome |
| $D_{it}$ | treated | 1 when treatment is active; otherwise 0 |
| $\alpha_i$ | district_id | Identifies districts for district fixed effects |
| $\lambda_t$ | year | Identifies years for year fixed effects |
| $\beta$ | Coefficient on treated | Estimated DID effect |
| $u_{it}$ | No input variable | Regression error |

Variables after the vertical bar specify fixed effects, not ordinary numeric predictors.
**data** selects the dataset; **vcov = ~ district_id** requests district-clustered standard errors.
The coefficient on treated equals the two-by-two contrast.
The true simulated effect is **2 points**, not necessarily the estimated value.

## 5. Estimate TWFE Using All Seven Years

The equation stays the same:

$$
Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\beta D_{it}+u_{it}
$$

```{r twfe}
model_twfe <- feols(
  outcome_raw ~ treated | district_id + year,
  data = simple,
  vcov = ~ district_id
)
summary(model_twfe)
```

Only **data = simple** changes: we now use all seven years.
District effects account for persistent differences; year effects account for common shocks.
In this balanced common-adoption design, the coefficient equals the treated group's average
pre-to-post change minus the control group's average change.
The true effect is **2 points in each post-treatment year**.
The time-constant treated_ever variable would be absorbed by district effects;
use treated, which switches on at adoption.

## 6. Estimate an Event Study

Following the slides:

$$
Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+
\sum_{k\neq-1}\beta_k\,\mathbf{1}\{t-g=k\}+u_{it}
$$

Here $g=5$ and $k=t-g$. The slides use shorthand: the event-time indicators apply to
treated districts, not the never-treated comparison group. Our code makes this restriction explicit.

| Study year | Event time | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 2, 3 | -4, -3, -2 | Pre-treatment comparisons |
| 4 | -1 | Reference period |
| 5, 6, 7 | 0, 1, 2 | First, second, third treated year |

```{r event-study}
simple <- simple %>%
  mutate(relative_year = year - 5)
model_event <- feols(
  outcome_raw ~ i(relative_year, treated_ever, ref = -1) |
    district_id + year,
  data = simple,
  vcov = ~ district_id
)
summary(model_event)
```

**mutate() is from dplyr.** This relative-year index is defined for every observation;
the existing event_time is missing for never-treated districts.
**i() from fixest** interacts relative-year indicators with treated_ever;
**ref = -1** omits Year 4.

Each $\beta_k$ measures how the treated-control gap differs from its Year 4 value.
Pre-treatment coefficients are diagnostics, not proof of parallel trends.
Under parallel trends and no anticipation, post-treatment coefficients estimate effects relative
to Year 4. Their true values are all **2 points** here.
Do not carry this common-adoption model mechanically into staggered adoption.

## 7. Move to Staggered Adoption

Effects now depend on cohort and year:

$$
\operatorname{ATT}(g,t)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{it}(g)-Y_{it}(0)\mid i\in G_g],
\qquad t\geq g
$$

$G_g$ is the cohort first treated in $g$; $Y_{it}(g)$ is the potential outcome when
treatment starts in $g$; $Y_{it}(0)$ is the outcome without treatment.

| Cohort $g$ | Year $t$ | True effect (points) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 5 | 1.00 |
| 5 | 6 | 2.00 |
| 5 | 7 | 3.00 |
| 6 | 6 | 1.50 |
| 6 | 7 | 2.50 |

These schedules are known effects added to the simulated untreated outcomes.
A single TWFE coefficient can mix never-treated, not-yet-treated, and already-treated comparisons.
Already-treated controls can be problematic when effects change over time.

## 8. Estimate Cohort-Time Treatment Effects

Use **att_gt() from did**, implementing
[Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001).
With never-treated controls:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}(g,t)
=(\overline Y_{g,t}-\overline Y_{g,g-1})
-(\overline Y_{C,t}-\overline Y_{C,g-1})
$$

ATT(6,7) compares the Year 6 cohort's change from Year 5 to Year 7
with the control group's change over those same years.

```{r csa}
set.seed(20261014)
model_csa <- att_gt(
  yname = "outcome_raw",
  tname = "year",
  idname = "district_id",
  gname = "treatment_start_year",
  xformla = ~ 1,
  data = staggered,
  panel = TRUE,
  control_group = "nevertreated",
  base_period = "universal",
  anticipation = 0,
  bstrap = TRUE,
  biters = 1000,
  clustervars = "district_id",
  cband = TRUE
)
summary(model_csa)
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| yname, tname, idname | Outcome, study-year, and district-ID columns |
| gname | First treatment year; 0 for never treated, not the binary treatment indicator |
| xformla = ~ 1 | No adjustment covariates |
| panel = TRUE | Follow the same districts over time |
| control_group = "nevertreated" | Use never-treated controls |
| base_period = "universal" | Reference each cohort's last untreated year |
| anticipation = 0 | No effects before adoption |

See the [att_gt() documentation](https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/reference/att_gt.html).

## 9. Read the Estimates and Uncertainty

**Group** identifies adoption cohort and **Time** identifies outcome year.
Group 5 and Time 7 identify ATT(5,7), whose true value is **3 points**.
Pre-treatment comparisons are diagnostics, not effects of an already-active treatment.

**bstrap = TRUE** uses a multiplier bootstrap; **biters = 1000** selects 1,000 iterations.
**clustervars = "district_id"** allows within-district dependence over time.
**set.seed()** makes the bootstrap reproducible in the same computing setup.

**cband = TRUE** requests simultaneous confidence bands across cohort-time estimates,
rather than separate pointwise intervals. See the
[did inference options](https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/reference/att_gt.html).

## 10. Aggregate the Cohort-Time Effects

Following the slides, the **Simple ATT** is:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}_{\mathrm{simple}}
=\sum_g\sum_{t=g}^{T}w_{g,t}\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}(g,t),
\qquad w_{g,t}=\frac{N_g}{\sum_h N_h(T-h+1)}
$$

$N_g$ is cohort size and $T=7$ is the final year.
This formula applies to our balanced panel without sampling weights.
The treated cohorts have equal size, so each of the five cells receives weight 1/5.
The true summary is:

$$
\operatorname{ATT}_{\mathrm{simple}}
=\frac{1.00+2.00+3.00+1.50+2.50}{5}=2.00
$$

```{r aggregation}
overall_csa <- aggte(model_csa, type = "simple")
summary(overall_csa)
```

**aggte() from did** takes the fitted model_csa object, not the original dataset.
**type = "simple"** selects the aggregation rule.
The early cohort contributes three post-treatment years and the late cohort two,
giving total weights 3/5 and 2/5. Never-treated districts supply the comparison,
but receive no treatment-effect weight. Do not average the five standard errors;
the package accounts for joint uncertainty.
See the [aggte() documentation](https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/reference/aggte.html).

Which effect summary answers your question? What makes parallel trends plausible?
